Physics and Simulation of a Cable-Park Wakeboard Rider

A detailed engineering analysis of tow-line mechanics, planing hydrodynamics, edging, rider dynamics, air-trick take-off, model hierarchy, numerical implementation, identification and validation.

Prepared 24 September 2026 · Focus: full-size cable parks and 2-tower cable systems, not boat wakeboarding · Language: English

Central thesis. Cable wakeboarding is best treated as a constrained, strongly nonlinear, hybrid multibody-fluid problem. The cable does not merely prescribe a rider speed. It injects power through a moving tether; the board redirects water momentum through an evolving, asymmetric planing contact; the rider actively changes the geometry and inertia of the system; and take-off or landing switches the system between contact regimes.

Abstract

This report develops a physics-based framework for simulating a wakeboard rider in a cable park. The treatment starts from first principles, then deliberately builds a hierarchy of reduced models suitable for real-time simulation, design studies, rider analysis and later high-fidelity validation. The most important cable-specific effects are the elevated tow point, the finite and usually taut line, the moving carrier, the possibility for rider speed to differ substantially from cable speed, the large line-load transients generated by progressive edging, and the absence of a boat-generated wake as the primary jump mechanism.

At ordinary riding speeds near 30 km/h, the board is in a high-Reynolds-number planing regime. The board is supported mainly by hydrodynamic pressure and, to a lesser extent, hydrostatic buoyancy. Its rolled and yawed attitude creates a three-dimensional force system. In a hard edge, the hydrodynamic resultant must simultaneously provide vertical support and substantial lateral force. The required force rises roughly as 1/cos(phi) in a simple banked-reaction picture, while the lateral component grows as tan(phi). That is why line load, spray, drag and rider acceleration can rise very quickly with edge angle.

For air tricks, the popular phrase “the water acts like a spring” is useful coaching shorthand but incomplete physics. The water stores little recoverable elastic energy at board scale. The dominant mechanism is an impulse generated by a large, rapidly reoriented hydrodynamic reaction, assisted by the upward component of line tension and powered ultimately by the cable drive. The board’s rocker, pitch, roll, yaw, contact area and release timing determine how horizontal momentum and cable work are converted into vertical and angular momentum.

1. Scope and cable-specific assumptions

The system of interest is a rider attached by a tow line to a moving carrier on an overhead cable. The primary regime is planing on approximately calm water, including straight riding, edging, carving, progressive line loading, cable-corner transitions and air-trick release. The report also discusses dock starts, landings and rigid features as hybrid extensions. It does not model a boat hull, a boat wake or propeller-driven flow.

Full-size cable parks commonly operate near 30 km/h. Official and competition material provides concrete examples with normal running speeds of 30 km/h and cable heights around 8.5 to 11.5 m. The 2026 IWWF Cable Wakeboard World Rules require the standard tow line at a full-size cable to be at least 17.80 m [10]. These are not universal constants, but they define a realistic design envelope for a reference simulation.

What makes cable physics different?

  • The pull point is high above the water, giving line tension a significant upward component.
  • The tow source follows a prescribed cable path rather than the rider’s path.
  • A taut line constrains relative motion but does not force rider speed to equal carrier speed.
  • The rider can swing around the moving carrier and temporarily exceed cable speed.
  • Air tricks can be generated by line loading and hydrodynamic release without a wake or kicker.
  • Carrier direction changes at towers introduce cable-specific transients.

What must not be imported blindly from boat wakeboarding?

  • Wake ramp geometry as the normal take-off mechanism.
  • Near-horizontal tow-line assumptions.
  • Boat-speed-equals-rider-speed reasoning.
  • Slalom-water-ski rope loads as direct cable-wakeboard data.
  • Symmetric planing-hull correlations as if a wakeboard were a rigid prismatic boat hull.

2. Cable geometry and kinematics

2.1 Coordinate systems

Use at least three frames:

  • Inertial frame I: X and Y horizontal, Z upward.
  • Carrier/path frame C: tangent along the local main-cable path, normal in the horizontal plane, vertical upward.
  • Board body frame B: xB along the board, yB across the board, zB approximately normal to the base.

The board attitude may be represented internally by a quaternion or rotation matrix to avoid Euler-angle singularities. Roll phi, pitch theta and yaw psi remain useful physical descriptors for interpretation.

2.2 Tow-line geometry

Figure 1. Reference cable geometry. An 18.5 m tow line with a 9 m vertical drop has a horizontal projection of about 16.2 m and a line elevation angle of about 29.1°. This is intentionally a representative example, not a universal park geometry.

Let c(t) be the carrier position and h(t) the handle position. Define the line vector, length and unit direction from handle to carrier as

r = c - h,    l = ||r||,    q = r / l.

For an ideal inextensible taut line of length L0, the holonomic constraint is

g(q) = ||c - h|| - L0 = 0.

Differentiating once gives the velocity constraint

q · (vc - vh) = 0.

This single equation destroys the common misconception that rider speed must equal cable speed. It constrains only the relative velocity component along the line. Tangential motion around the carrier is free. Consequently, the rider can move faster or slower than the carrier while the line remains taut.

2.3 Elastic line alternative

If tow-line stretch, handle elasticity and cable compliance matter, replace the exact constraint with a unilateral spring-damper law:

T = max[0, kr(l-L0) + cr dl/dt].

The max operator is important because a rope can pull but cannot push. In a production simulator the line should therefore be represented either as a unilateral compliant element or as a complementarity constraint with a slack/tight event.

3. Complete force inventory

For a combined rider-board body, the external forces are:

ForcePhysical originDirection and modelling notes
GravityEarthm g downward through the system centre of mass.
Tow-line tensionCable drive and tetherT q at the handle. Produces both translational force and a moment about the centre of mass.
Hydrodynamic pressureWater momentum redirectionDistributed over the instantaneous wetted footprint. Dominant support force while planing.
Viscous shearBoundary layerApproximately tangential to the board surface and opposite local water-relative motion.
Spray and wave-making dragFree-surface flowMomentum carried by spray sheets and waves. Difficult to capture with a simple skin-friction model.
Hydrostatic buoyancyDisplaced waterImportant at low speed and during starts; reduced relative importance in fast planing.
Fin / edge forcesSeparated 3D flow and appendagesCan alter yaw stability, side force and drag. Cable boards may be finless or use small fins.
Aerodynamic dragAirUsually secondary on-water, but relevant in flight and for rider posture.
Feature/contact forcesKicker, rail, slider, dockUnilateral normal force plus friction, possibly impulsive.

The exact fluid force is the surface integral

Ffluid = -∫Sw p n dS + ∫Sw τ · n dS,

with a corresponding moment integral about the chosen reference point. A master-level simulation should be explicit about which parts of this integral are modelled physically, which are empirical closures and which are neglected.

Figure 3A. Conceptual free-body diagram. The actual hydrodynamic force is a distributed pressure/shear field and the tow-line force acts at the hands, not at the COM. The diagram is therefore a force-bookkeeping aid rather than a substitute for moment equations.

3.1 Translational versus rotational consequences

A force inventory alone is not enough. The same force can produce very different rider behaviour depending on where it acts. The line tension is applied at the handle; the board-water pressure acts over a moving centre of pressure; gravity acts through the total centre of mass; and binding forces transfer load between board and rider. The net force controls centre-of-mass acceleration, while the net moment controls pitch, roll and yaw.

aCOM = ΣF / m,    and    H_dotCOM = Σ[(ri-rCOM) × Fi] + ΣMi.

This is especially important during air-trick initiation. Two manoeuvres may have almost the same total upward force but very different angular acceleration because the board’s centre of pressure and the handle position differ.

3.2 Order-of-magnitude force scale

For an 80 kg rider-board system, body weight is about 785 N. At 30 km/h the water dynamic pressure is about 34.7 kPa, so the fluid does not need to act over the full board area at high average pressure to support the rider. If an effective wetted area is roughly 0.25 to 0.35 m², an average net supporting pressure of only a few kilopascals is enough to carry body weight. Local peak pressures near the spray root can be much higher than this area-average value.

Air drag on the rider is usually smaller than water and line forces while planing. In flight, a rough scale 0.5 rho_air C_D A U² with rho_air around 1.2 kg/m³, C_D A around 0.5 to 0.8 m² and U around 10 m/s gives tens of newtons. That is not dominant compared with gravity or a heavily loaded tow line, but it can affect long flight phases and body orientation.

4. Planing hydrodynamics of the wakeboard

4.1 Flow regime

Using water density 1000 kg/m³, kinematic viscosity 10⁻⁶ m²/s, board length 1.42 m and 30 km/h, the reference dimensionless numbers are:

1.18e+07
Reynolds number, Re = U L / nu
2.23
length Froude number, Fr = U / sqrt(gL)
4.06
beam Froude number, based on 0.43 m width
34.7 kPa
dynamic pressure q = 1/2 rho U²
Figure 2. Froude numbers over a practical speed range. Froude scaling is central because gravity and free-surface deformation compete with inertial pressure forces.
Figure 3. Reynolds number is of order 10⁷ at normal full-size cable speed. The board boundary layer and separated edge flow are therefore predominantly turbulent.

The Weber number of the reference case is approximately 1.37e+06, so surface tension is negligible for the global force balance. It still influences spray breakup and droplets, but not the primary rider dynamics.

4.2 Pressure generation

A planing surface at positive trim deflects water downward and sideways. Near the forward wetting line, the flow decelerates and the local pressure rises strongly. Water then accelerates beneath and away from the board, forming spray roots and sheets. The integrated pressure field produces a resultant approximately normal to the local wetted surface, but its line of action moves as speed, trim, roll, yaw, rocker and load change.

Savitsky’s classic planing relations were developed for prismatic planing hulls [1,2]. They are useful as a dimensional and numerical baseline, not as a literal wakeboard law. A commonly used flat-surface relation is

CL0 = tau1.1[0.012 lambda1/2 + 0.0055 lambda5/2 / CV²],

where lambda is a mean wetted-length-to-width ratio and CV = U/sqrt(gB). The 2024 review by Tavakoli et al. summarises the scope and limitations of such empirical methods and the broader analytical, numerical and CFD literature [1].

Figure 4. A Savitsky-type flat-plate baseline for the reference vertical load. Lower trim requires a longer wetted footprint to generate the same support. The wakeboard’s rocker, flex, finite tips, roll and yaw mean that this plot should be treated as a starting approximation only.

4.3 Pressure drag and skin friction

For a small trim angle, the pressure resultant is tilted backward. A useful first-order estimate is

Dpressure ≈ N tan(tau).

Skin-friction drag may be approximated by

Df = 1/2 rho U² Sw Cf,    Cf ≈ 0.075 / [log10(Re)-2]²,

with the ITTC-57 correlation used only as a convenient turbulent flat-plate closure. Spray drag, three-dimensional edge losses, fin drag and separated-flow losses should be modelled as separate residual terms or identified from data.

4.4 Why a wakeboard is harder than a standard planing hull

  • Rocker: the base is curved in the longitudinal direction, so local incidence varies strongly along the board.
  • Flex: cable boards can deform under foot loads and hydrodynamic pressure, changing rocker dynamically.
  • Roll and yaw: edging is inherently unsymmetrical planing. Classical NACA work measured all three forces and all three moments under roll and yaw [3].
  • Finite rounded tips: there is no conventional transom boundary condition.
  • Foot loading: two concentrated binding loads alter bending and local immersion.
  • Ventilation and spray: a deeply edged board may entrain air and develop asymmetric wetting.

These effects make unsteady strip methods, asymmetric 2D+T methods and CFD increasingly attractive as fidelity increases [4-6].

4.5 Free-surface governing equations

At the highest fidelity, the water phase is governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with a moving free surface:

∇ · u = 0,
rho [∂u/∂t + (u · ∇)u] = -∇p + mu ∇²u + rho g.

At the air-water interface, pressure and shear stresses must be matched and the interface must move with the fluid. In a Volume-of-Fluid formulation an indicator field alphaw is transported with

∂alphaw/∂t + ∇ · (alphaw u) = 0,

with alphaw near 1 in water and near 0 in air. The board boundary imposes no-penetration and, in viscous CFD, no-slip. A freely moving board then adds a two-way coupled rigid-body or fluid-structure-interaction problem.

For wakeboarding, the numerically difficult region is not the far field. It is the moving wetting line, thin spray sheet, intermittent ventilation at the edge and the fast change in wetted topology during release and landing. These phenomena are why a CFD result can look visually plausible while still producing the wrong integrated force unless mesh, time step, turbulence closure and interface treatment are carefully verified.

4.6 Rocker as a local angle-of-attack distribution

Let the undeformed board base be represented by zb(x,y) = r(x) + c(y), where r(x) is longitudinal rocker and c(y) captures channels or transverse curvature. Add flexible deformation using modal coordinates etai:

zb(x,y,t) = r(x) + c(y) + Σ etai(t) Phii(x,y).

The local bottom slope changes the effective incidence seen by each strip. For small angles, a useful kinematic estimate is

alphaeff(x) ≈ theta + dr/dx + wrel(x)/U,

where wrel includes heave, pitch-rate and wave-elevation contributions. This explains why two boards with identical overall length and width can have materially different pressure distributions even at the same COM trim angle.

4.7 Strip-theory route between empirical formulas and CFD

A pragmatic middle model divides the board into transverse strips. Each strip is treated as a local water-entry / planing section with its own effective entry velocity, wetted half-width and local roll. Section forces are integrated along the board:

FH = ∫ fsection(x) dx,    MH = ∫ [r(x)-rCOM] × fsection(x) dx.

This route naturally produces a moving centre of pressure and can incorporate added mass. Its weakness is that 3D cross-flow, ventilation and tip effects are only approximate. Tveitnes’ work is particularly relevant because it highlights the difficulty of using added-mass ideas consistently during both water entry and exit [4].

4.8 Hydrodynamic coefficient maps for real-time simulation

For M2 real-time simulation, the most practical architecture is often a smooth coefficient map rather than a single analytic equation. One possible parameterisation is

[CX, CY, CZ, Cl, Cm, Cn] = f(phi, theta, beta, Fr, Re, h/L, p/U, q/U, r/U),

where p, q and r denote roll, pitch and yaw rates. The map can be built from experiments, CFD or both, and then regularised so that symmetry, passivity and known limiting behaviour are respected.

Figure 4A. Example of what a calibrated side-force coefficient map could look like as a function of edge angle and sideslip. The numbers shown are synthetic. The point is the modelling structure: roll and yaw/sideslip should be independent state variables, not collapsed into a single “edge coefficient”.

5. Edge mechanics and carving

5.1 The simplest useful picture

Suppose the hydrodynamic resultant N is approximately normal to the board base and the board is rolled by an edge angle phi. Ignoring pitch for a moment, its vertical and lateral components are approximately

Fz ≈ N cos(phi),    Fy ≈ N sin(phi).

If the required water-supported vertical load is Weff, then

N ≈ Weff / cos(phi),    Fy ≈ Weff tan(phi).
Figure 5. The basic geometry explains why strong edging is expensive in force. At 35° roll, the required normal reaction is about 22% larger than at zero roll, while the lateral component is about 70% of the water-supported weight. At 45°, lateral reaction equals the water-supported weight in this idealised picture.

5.2 Side force, yaw and the “rail” effect

A real board does not simply bank like an aircraft. It also has yaw relative to the water velocity, curved rocker, finite edge sharpness and possibly fins. Therefore the lateral force depends on both roll and sideslip. A practical reduced model can use

Y = 1/2 rho U² Seff CY(phi, beta, theta, Re, Fr, rocker),

where beta is the board-water sideslip angle. NACA unsymmetrical-planing experiments and later yawed-planing models show that roll and yaw affect lift, drag, side force and all three moments, which supports treating cable edging as a genuinely 6-DOF hydrodynamic problem [3,5,6].

5.3 Turning radius

If Flat,net is the net horizontal force normal to the rider velocity, the instantaneous curvature is

kappa = Flat,net / (m U²),    R = 1/kappa.

The tow line may contribute either toward or away from the centre of curvature depending on where the rider is relative to the carrier. Therefore a line load cannot be converted directly into “turning force” without geometry.

5.4 Progressive edging and speed gain

The cable rider can gain speed by swinging around the translating carrier. If the horizontal rope projection r is approximately constant and psi is the azimuth of the rider behind the carrier, then

vrider = Vc ex + r psi_dot et.

The second term is a tangential swing velocity. This is the cable analogue of the speed build-up familiar from slalom water skiing, although the elevated tow point and cable path make the geometry different.

Figure 6. Top view of a synthetic constrained-pendulum carve. Thin connecting lines show the tow line at selected times. The model is intentionally low-order and is used to expose geometry, not to claim measured performance.
Figure 7. In the same synthetic model, the rider accelerates from the 30 km/h carrier speed to above 40 km/h while loading the edge. This is possible because the taut line constrains radial relative velocity, not total speed.

5.5 Derivation of the planar moving-tether model

On a straight cable span, assume for the moment that the vertical line angle is constant and the horizontal line projection has length r. Let psi measure the rider’s horizontal swing angle behind the carrier. The rider position is

xr = xc - r cos(psi),    yr = -r sin(psi).

With x_dotc = Vc, differentiation gives

vr = [Vc + r psi_dot sin(psi),   -r psi_dot cos(psi)].

A second differentiation decomposes acceleration into a radial part r psi_dot² toward the carrier and a tangential part r psi_ddot. Projecting Newton’s law onto the tangential direction eliminates line tension because the tension is radial:

m r psi_ddot = Fhydro · et.

Projecting radially gives the horizontal line-tension component:

Th = m r psi_dot² - Fhydro · etow.

This two-equation system is exceptionally useful for intuition. It shows that edging creates tangential acceleration, while the increasing swing rate creates the centripetal line load m r psi_dot². It also shows why line tension can rise even if drag does not rise proportionally.

5.6 Maximum speed is not set by cable speed alone

The kinematic formula above implies that rider speed depends on the vector sum of carrier translation and swing velocity. There is no simple universal maximum. The achievable speed is bounded instead by the available hydrodynamic side force, drag, rope geometry, rider strength/control, line tension, park clearance and the finite duration of the carve. A model that hard-clamps U = Vc therefore suppresses one of the central mechanisms of cable riding.

5.7 Cavitation is normally not the first limiting fluid mechanism

At wakeboard speeds, global static pressure is far above vapour pressure. Local negative pressures can occur in separated and ventilated regions, but air ventilation from the free surface is generally more accessible than classical fully submerged cavitation. For reduced modelling, ventilation and loss of wetted area are usually more relevant first-order effects than a cavitation model.

6. Rider biomechanics and multibody coupling

The rider is not passive ballast. Body posture changes the system centre of mass, moments of inertia, handle location, binding loads, board pitch and board flex. A realistic simulator should distinguish at least three levels:

Rider representationStatesUse
Lumped mass at fixed COMNone beyond board poseFast force-balance studies and control prototypes.
Rigid rider body connected to boardRelative trunk angle, handle pointPitch/roll moment studies and basic take-off.
Articulated multibody riderHip, knee, ankle, shoulder, elbow, trunk jointsTechnique, joint loads, trick initiation and landing biomechanics.

In an articulated model, joint torques are control inputs. The board receives foot forces and moments through the bindings, while the line load enters through the hands. This creates a closed mechanical chain: cable → arms → torso → legs → board → water.

A useful formulation is a floating-base multibody system with generalized coordinates q and velocities u:

M(q) u_dot + C(q,u) + G(q) = Qmuscle + JlineT lambdaline + JwaterT lambdawater.

For performance analysis, the “control” problem is then to find a joint-torque and edge-angle history that achieves a target path or trick while respecting joint limits, force limits and line-tension constraints.

6.1 Segmental centre of mass and inertia

For an articulated rider, the whole-body centre of mass is

rCOM = (1/M) Σ mi ri.

When the rider extends the legs, leans away from the handle or moves the arms, rCOM can shift by several tenths of a metre relative to the board. That shift changes the pitch and roll moments required from the water. In flight, changing body configuration changes the inertia tensor and therefore angular speed even if total angular momentum is nearly conserved.

6.2 Internal versus external angular momentum

Joint torques are internal to the rider-board system and cannot by themselves change the total angular momentum of an isolated system. They can redistribute it between body segments and change rotation rate by changing inertia. The tow line and aerodynamic forces are external, so they can change total angular momentum in flight. This distinction is crucial for cable tricks because a rider is not a free projectile as long as the line remains loaded.

6.3 Foot-pressure control

Front- and rear-foot loading influence board pitch, flex and wetted footprint. A minimal control model can use two normal binding forces Ffront and Frear subject to

Ffront + Frear ≈ transmitted vertical rider load,

with their difference generating a pitch moment. In a flexible-board model these forces also excite bending modes. This is a better physical control variable than prescribing board pitch directly if the aim is to reproduce rider technique.

6.4 Inverse dynamics from measured motion

Once board and body motion are measured, inverse dynamics can estimate the net hydrodynamic wrench required to explain the motion:

Whydro,est = Winertial - Wgravity - Wline - Waero.

This is an attractive identification route because the water force does not have to be measured directly. The weakness is sensitivity to acceleration and angular-acceleration noise, so high-rate IMUs and careful filtering are essential.

7. Governing equations of motion

7.1 6-DOF rigid board+rider model

For a combined rigid body with centre-of-mass position x, velocity v, angular velocity omega and body inertia I:

m v_dot = m g + Fline + Fhydro + Faero + Fcontact,
I omega_dot + omega × (I omega) = Mline + Mhydro + Maero + Mcontact.

The tow-line moment is not optional. Because the handle is usually well above and forward of the combined COM, line tension can strongly affect pitch and roll.

7.2 Water force closure

At reduced order, write the hydrodynamic wrench as

WH = H(U, phi, theta, beta, heave, angular rates, wetted state, rocker, flex, roughness).

The model may include static coefficient maps plus unsteady terms:

FH = FQS + Ahyd(q) a + Bhyd(q) v + Fslam.

Ahyd represents added-mass effects. These become important during water entry, rapid pitch/heave and release. Added-mass theory for planing surfaces is nontrivial because the wetted region itself changes and because entry and exit are not symmetric [4].

7.3 Differential-algebraic structure

With an inextensible line and hard water/contact constraints, the simulator is naturally a differential-algebraic equation (DAE). Lagrange multipliers can represent line tension and contact reactions. Alternatively, penalty springs simplify implementation but introduce stiffness and tuning parameters.

7.4 Solving line tension as a Lagrange multiplier

Let the handle be part of a multibody state with generalized coordinates q. The inextensible line constraint can be written C(q,t)=0. Constrained dynamics have the standard form

M(q) q_ddot + h(q,q_dot) = Q + JT lambda,
J q_ddot + J_dot q_dot + Ctt = 0.

The scalar multiplier lambda associated with the line constraint is the generalized constraint force, from which physical tow tension is recovered. Numerically this can be solved as a saddle-point system each time step. Compared with a very stiff spring, the DAE formulation avoids artificial rope oscillations and gives a cleaner tension signal.

7.5 Complementarity for slack line

An exact rope model is unilateral. Define gap g = L0 - l. A slack rope has T=0 and g>0, while a taut rope has g=0 and T>=0. This can be written as a complementarity condition

T ≥ 0,    g ≥ 0,    T g = 0.

That formulation is valuable for starts, failed tricks and corner transients where the rope may briefly unload.

7.6 Water contact as another unilateral system

The board-water interface is also unilateral in a reduced contact formulation: water can push on the board through pressure but cannot sustain tensile contact after separation. This means take-off is fundamentally a contact-release event, not merely a continuous decrease in a lift coefficient.

8. Energy and power flow

8.1 Cable power input

For a taut, inextensible line, q · (vc-vh) = 0. Therefore q · vh = q · vc. The instantaneous power delivered to the rider through the line is

Pline = T q · vh = T q · vc.

This result is important. The energy source is the moving cable drive. The rider can have a speed larger than the cable speed while the motor still supplies energy through the projection of carrier velocity onto the line direction.

8.2 Dissipation

Hydrodynamic drag dissipates mechanical energy into turbulence, waves, spray and heat. A model with lateral hydrodynamic force exactly perpendicular to velocity does no work through that lateral term, while drag contributes approximately -D U. Real board forces are not perfectly orthogonal, so carving also increases dissipative power.

Figure 8. Synthetic carve example. Tow-line tension and cable-to-rider power both rise during progressive loading. The numerical values are illustrative and depend on the deliberately simple side-force and drag closures.

8.3 Energy accounting as a debugging tool

For any simulator, monitor

d/dt (K + Ugravity + Eelastic) = Pline + Prider - Pdissipation + Pcontacts.

If the numerical model creates large unexplained energy, the likely causes are inconsistent constraint forces, a sign error in hydrodynamic moments, too-stiff penalty contacts or discontinuous coefficient maps.

8.4 Derivation of cable power identity

Because the line is inextensible, the endpoint velocities have equal components along the line: q · vh = q · vc. The force on the handle is Tq, hence

Prider = (Tq) · vh = T q · vc.

The equality does not say that the rider and carrier have equal speed. It says the line transmits power consistently with the geometric constraint. In a straight span with carrier speed Vc and horizontal line azimuth psi, the approximate power is Th Vc cos(psi). As the rider swings farther to the side, the projection can decrease even while tension increases.

8.5 Where the rider’s muscular work enters

Human joint torques do mechanical work internally and against the board/handle. The rider can absorb energy, for example by bending the knees on landing, or redistribute mechanical energy by changing posture. In a full biomechanical model, joint power Pj = tauj q_dotj should be tracked separately from cable power and fluid dissipation.

9. Air-trick take-off: line loading, release and impulse

9.1 Physical sequence

  1. Approach: rider travels with moderate edge and taut line.
  2. Progressive load: increased roll/yaw creates larger lateral hydrodynamic reaction, tension and often greater rider speed.
  3. Scoop / release: board pitch, edge and contact footprint change rapidly. The pressure resultant rotates and may increase sharply.
  4. Loss of water contact: wetted area collapses. The system switches from planing dynamics to tethered flight.
  5. Flight: gravity, line tension and aerodynamic forces dominate; rider joint motion redistributes angular momentum.

Practical cable-wakeboard instruction describes this as building line tension and then releasing the edge to initiate air tricks [11]. The mechanics interpretation is an impulse and energy-redirection process, not simply stored elastic energy in water.

9.2 Linear impulse

Across a short take-off interval [t₀,t₁],

m(v1-v0) = ∫[Fhydro + Fline + mg] dt.

The vertical part is

m Δvz = Jhydro,z + Jline,z - mg Δt.

The upward line component can be substantial in a cable park because the tow point is elevated. This is one reason boat-derived near-horizontal line models are unsuitable.

Figure 9. Ballistic-equivalent jump height versus net vertical take-off impulse for an 80 kg system. This plot is a diagnostic, not a full air-trick prediction. Continued tow-line work during flight can materially change the trajectory.

9.3 Angular impulse

Rotation is generated by moments of the water force, tow-line force and active rider torques:

H1-H0 = ∫ Mexternal dt.

Where the hydrodynamic centre of pressure sits relative to the combined COM is therefore critical. A small change in rocker contact, front-foot pressure or release timing can change the angular impulse even if the total vertical impulse remains similar.

9.4 A better model of “pop”

A useful reduced take-off model should include: time-varying wetted length, board pitch rate, roll, yaw, a rocker-dependent centre of pressure, an unsteady added-mass term, tow-line geometry and a contact-loss event. A static lift coefficient alone will generally under-predict the sharp transient at release.

9.5 Airborne tethered dynamics

After water contact vanishes, the translational equation becomes approximately

m a = m g + T q + Faero.

If the line remains taut, the same line-length constraint still applies and tension must provide whatever radial acceleration is required by the rider’s three-dimensional motion. The flight is therefore closer to a driven spherical pendulum with a translating suspension point than to a ballistic projectile.

The ballistic-equivalent height in Figure 9 is still useful because it converts measured take-off vertical velocity into an intuitive energy scale. But a full prediction should integrate the tethered flight equations, including continued work by the carrier and line moments about the rider-board COM.

9.6 Release timing and centre-of-pressure migration

Suppose the hydrodynamic resultant grows during loading but its centre of pressure moves aft as the nose unloads. The same force magnitude then creates a rapidly changing pitch moment. A physically convincing take-off model therefore needs both force magnitude and force application point. Fitting only total line tension cannot identify this moment distribution uniquely.

9.7 Why the board may leave the water upward

There is no violation of “water only pushes”. Immediately before separation, the board has a finite upward normal velocity and receives a positive normal impulse from the pressure field. When the local gap velocity becomes positive everywhere, pressure contact collapses. The upward momentum already acquired carries the board into flight. The cable’s upward force can then continue to add vertical momentum while the line remains loaded.

10. Cable corners and carrier dynamics

A full-size cable consists of straight spans joined by tower sheaves. Even if cable speed magnitude is constant, the carrier velocity direction changes. On an ideal circular corner of radius Rc, carrier centripetal acceleration is Vc²/Rc. The tow-line endpoint therefore has a nonzero prescribed acceleration, and the rider must follow through line tension and water force.

A corner model should include:

  • piecewise carrier path c(s) with continuous tangent if possible,
  • measured or manufacturer-derived corner radius,
  • cable/carrier compliance to avoid unrealistically instantaneous direction changes,
  • tower-induced line-angle changes,
  • rider pre-position relative to the corner buoy,
  • possible transient slack or snap load.

For park-specific simulation, measuring the actual carrier trajectory with video, total-station survey or RTK GNSS is more valuable than guessing a generic polygon.

10.1 Full-size cable versus 2-tower systems

AspectFull-size loop2-tower system
Carrier motionContinuous loop with repeated tower cornersBack-and-forth motion with reversals at ends
Speed controlUsually nearly constant during public ridingOften programmable acceleration, deceleration and reversal
Key transientDirection change at sheaves / cornersEnd-of-line deceleration and launch/reversal
Traffic couplingMultiple carriers and riders share main cable dynamicsUsually one rider, more isolated system
Best first modelPrescribed closed carrier pathPrescribed 1D carrier trajectory with acceleration limits

10.2 Main-cable compliance and drive dynamics

The simplest model prescribes carrier motion exactly. A higher-fidelity cable model adds main-cable elasticity, pretension, sag, carrier mass, sheave geometry and motor control. Rider load then perturbs the cable itself. If the drive is speed-regulated, the motor controller responds with torque to reject that disturbance. For a park with several riders, their loads are coupled through the same moving cable. This is mechanically interesting but should be added only if measured carrier speed shows deviations that matter to the rider dynamics.

11. Starts, landings and features as hybrid dynamics

11.1 Dock and deep-water starts

At low speed the board is displacement-dominated and partially submerged. As speed rises, dynamic pressure grows with U² and the board transitions to planing. A single high-speed planing coefficient map should not be extrapolated through zero speed. The start regime needs buoyancy, form drag, changing immersion and potentially added-mass terms.

11.2 Landings

Landing is a water-entry impact. Normal velocity of the board drives an added-mass/slamming load that may be several times the steady planing force for a short period. The force depends strongly on local deadrise-equivalent geometry, roll, pitch, rocker and entry velocity. This is exactly the kind of regime where water-entry theory and CFD become more defensible than steady Savitsky-style relations [4].

11.3 Kickers and rails

A kicker is a rigid contact surface that replaces part of the hydrodynamic support with a contact normal force. Rails and sliders create frictional contact and may involve board flex. These are naturally modelled with event-driven contact mechanics. They can be added after the open-water cable model is validated, rather than mixed into the first model from day one.

12. Recommended model hierarchy

LevelCore physicsTypical runtimeBest use
M0: algebraic force balanceSteady vertical and drag balance; prescribed attitudemicrosecondsSanity checks, parameter sizing, interactive teaching.
M1: point mass + taut line2D/3D rider trajectory, drag, edge side force, cable geometryreal timeCarving, speed gain, line-load intuition.
M2: 6-DOF rigid board+riderHydrodynamic force/moment maps, line moment, contact eventsreal time to faster-than-real-timeControl studies, take-off and landing envelopes.
M3: articulated rider + flexible boardMultibody rider, binding loads, modal board flex0.1× to real timeTechnique, joint loading, trick initiation.
M4: unsteady strip / 2D+T hydroChanging wetting, added mass, asymmetric entry/exitseconds to minutes per second simulatedHydrodynamic model development.
M5: CFD/VOF + FSIFree surface, spray, ventilation, board motion/flexhours to daysHigh-fidelity validation and coefficient generation.
Recommended engineering route. Build M1 and M2 first, instrument a rider, fit the unknown hydrodynamic coefficients, then use M4/M5 selectively to understand where the reduced model fails. Starting directly with CFD is computationally impressive but scientifically risky if the rider control inputs, board flex and line loads are unknown.

13. Numerical implementation

13.1 State vector

A practical M2 state is

x = [position, velocity, quaternion, angular velocity, line state, wetted-state variables].

For M3, append rider joint angles and rates plus flexible-board modal coordinates.

13.2 Integration

  • Use quaternion or rotation-matrix integration with normalisation.
  • Use event detection for water contact loss, re-entry, line slack/tight transitions and feature impacts.
  • For compliant lines and contact, an implicit or semi-implicit solver can be more stable than naïve explicit Euler.
  • Typical reduced-order on-water integration may tolerate 1 to 5 ms steps. Impacts may require substantially smaller steps or impulse-based treatment.

13.3 Hydrodynamic lookup architecture

Do not hard-code one drag coefficient. Use a model interface that can later be swapped:

hydro_wrench = hydro_model(
    water_relative_velocity,
    board_attitude,
    angular_velocity,
    heave_state,
    board_geometry,
    flex_state,
    calibrated_parameters
)

The first implementation can be a smooth coefficient map. The same interface can later call a neural surrogate trained on CFD, a strip-theory solver or a precomputed multidimensional table.

13.4 Constraint handling

Three sensible options exist:

  1. Exact DAE: solve line tension as a Lagrange multiplier.
  2. Stiff compliant line: simple, but introduces artificial high-frequency dynamics.
  3. Projection method: integrate unconstrained motion, then project position/velocity back onto the line constraint. Good for real-time prototypes if energy error is monitored.

13.5 Numerical stiffness and event resolution

Three mechanisms generate fast time scales: rope compliance, water-entry impact and rigid feature contact. If all are represented by stiff penalty springs, the stable explicit time step can become impractically small. Better options are exact line constraints, impulse-based contact and an unsteady hydrodynamic model whose time constants are physically motivated.

A useful numerical test is time-step convergence. Repeat the same manoeuvre at dt, dt/2 and dt/4. Quantities such as peak tension and landing impulse should converge. If the peak doubles as the time step shrinks, the model may contain an unresolved discontinuity rather than a physical load.

13.6 Smoothness of empirical maps

Hydrodynamic coefficient interpolation must be at least continuously differentiable if the model is used for optimisation, parameter estimation or gradient-based control. Piecewise tables with sharp slope changes can create artificial jerks that the solver interprets as physics. Monotone cubic interpolation, Gaussian-process surrogates with constraints or differentiable neural surrogates are better candidates than raw nearest-neighbour lookup.

13.7 Simulation observability outputs

Log more than state variables. A useful trace includes line tension, cable power, hydrodynamic force and moment components, wetted area, centre of pressure, each energy term, constraint residuals and contact state. These internal channels are what make a physics simulator scientifically diagnosable instead of merely visual.

Figure 10. Order-of-magnitude force budget for the reference straight-running case. This estimate uses a flat-plate planing closure, ITTC-style friction and a small residual drag term. It is not calibrated wakeboard data.

The implied mean wetted length is about 0.87 m. This is plausible in magnitude, but it should not be interpreted literally because a real cable board has rocker and an asymmetric wet footprint.

14.3 Synthetic progressive edge

To expose the geometry, a point-mass rider was constrained to a fixed horizontal line projection of 16.2 m. A smooth edge command rose to 38° and then released. A simple side-force closure generated lateral water force; drag increased with edge load. The resulting rider speed peaked at 44.0 km/h and tow tension at 706 N.

Do not treat these peak numbers as experimental predictions. They are outputs from a pedagogical reduced model. Their purpose is to demonstrate the mechanism by which lateral swing, line tension, cable power and speed couple. Actual cable-wakeboard force histories must be measured and used for identification.

15. Measurement and parameter identification

15.1 Minimum instrument set

MeasurementSensorWhy it matters
Tow-line tensionInline load cell at handle or ropeMost direct observable of cable-rider coupling.
Board attitude and accelerationHigh-rate IMU on boardRoll, pitch, yaw rates, impact timing and inertial forces.
Rider/board trajectoryRTK GNSS or fused GNSS + IMUSpeed gain, path curvature and line geometry.
Carrier position/speedCable encoder or vision trackingRequired to compute relative kinematics and cable power.
VideoHigh-frame-rate shore camerasWetted footprint, posture, release timing, validation.
Board strain / flexStrain gauges or fibre sensorsDynamic rocker and binding load distribution.
Optional pressureFlush miniature pressure sensorsDirect validation of local planing pressure, difficult but high value.

15.2 Identification sequence

  1. Calibrate geometry, mass and inertia on land.
  2. Measure straight riding at several cable speeds to fit baseline drag and vertical-support parameters.
  3. Run controlled constant-edge-angle traverses to identify side-force and roll/yaw moment maps.
  4. Run progressive-edge manoeuvres to identify unsteady terms and line/cable compliance.
  5. Instrument basic ollies and then air tricks to identify release impulse and centre-of-pressure migration.
  6. Validate on riders and boards not used for fitting.

15.3 What existing water-ski data can and cannot tell us

Biomechanical studies of slalom water skiing have measured running and cutting rope loads. Intermediate-ski studies reported average running rope loads around 0.35 to 0.41 body weight and start peaks up to 2.45 body weight [7]. An advanced-skier study reported typical average peak cutting loads of roughly 1.41 to 2.74 body weight [8]. These data are useful for sensor-range selection and for appreciating that tow-line loads can become large. They should not be transplanted as cable-wakeboard coefficients because the board geometry, tow height, manoeuvres and rider mechanics are different.

15.4 Proposed experimental protocol

A controlled campaign could use one experienced rider and one board first, then expand to multiple riders. Each run should begin with 10 to 15 seconds of steady riding for sensor bias estimation. Suggested manoeuvre blocks are: straight ride, fixed mild edge, fixed moderate edge, repeated S-turns, progressive edge without take-off, loaded ollie, basic air trick and controlled landing.

For line-load capture, use at least a few hundred hertz sample rate and sufficient overload margin. A 3 to 5 kN load-cell range is a sensible instrumentation class for research because published slalom-ski peaks can exceed twice body weight [7,8], even though cable-wakeboard peaks must be measured rather than assumed from those studies. Board IMU data should preferably be 200 Hz or higher, while high-speed video around 240 fps provides useful release and landing timing. The channels should be hardware-synchronised or aligned to within a few milliseconds.

15.5 State estimation

GNSS alone is poor at high-frequency acceleration. IMU alone drifts. Fuse them using an extended Kalman filter or smoothing estimator. Add known rope length and carrier position as geometric information. Video can provide an external attitude/trajectory reference for selected runs and helps detect IMU saturation at landing.

15.6 Parameter estimation as an optimisation problem

Let theta denote the unknown hydro and line parameters. Estimate them by minimising a weighted residual over multiple experiments:

theta* = arg min Σruns Σk || ymeas(k) - ysim(k;theta) ||W² + R(theta).

The regularisation R(theta) should encode physical priors such as positive drag, smooth coefficients and symmetry. Fitting all parameters to one aggressive manoeuvre is a bad identification strategy because many parameter combinations can reproduce the same line-tension trace.

16. Validation strategy

A credible master-level model should be judged on several independent observables rather than “the animation looks right”. Recommended metrics include:

  • RMS and peak error in line tension.
  • RMS board roll, pitch and yaw-rate error.
  • Trajectory error in the horizontal plane.
  • Peak rider speed and timing relative to edge command.
  • Take-off vertical velocity and angular velocity.
  • Landing normal acceleration and impulse.
  • Energy-balance residual.
  • Generalisation across rider mass, board size, speed and line geometry.

Separate calibration and validation datasets. Otherwise the model may simply absorb rider technique into hydrodynamic coefficients and appear more physical than it is.

16.1 Hierarchical validation

Validate each submodel before the full system. First verify tow-line geometry against static measurements. Then validate straight-planing drag and vertical support. Next validate lateral force using controlled traverses. Only then evaluate aggressive loading and take-off. This prevents an error in one subsystem from being accidentally cancelled by another fitted parameter.

16.2 Cross-validation across boards and riders

A robust model should preserve its hydrodynamic parameters when rider mass changes, while rider-control parameters may change. Likewise, changing board geometry should alter the board coefficients but not cable stiffness. This separation is a powerful test of whether identified parameters have physical meaning.

16.3 Validation against force and motion simultaneously

A model that matches trajectory but misses line tension can still be dynamically wrong; a model that matches tension but misses board attitude can have the wrong centre of pressure. Require simultaneous agreement in at least one force channel and several kinematic channels.

17. Uncertainty and sensitivity

The dominant uncertainties are likely to be:

  1. Rider control inputs: joint torques and posture are difficult to measure and can dominate the result.
  2. Wetted footprint: changes rapidly with rocker, roll, pitch, yaw, speed and wave state.
  3. Board flex: can alter local incidence and pressure distribution.
  4. Line/cable compliance: affects peak tension and phase.
  5. Water roughness and wind: perturb entry, spray and rider control.
  6. Hydrodynamic centre of pressure: a small location error creates a large pitch/roll moment error.
  7. Contact-event timing: take-off and landing are sensitive to millisecond-scale phase differences.

Use uncertainty propagation rather than one “best” trajectory. Monte Carlo or polynomial-chaos studies over uncertain hydro coefficients, rider timing and line stiffness can show which measurements most reduce prediction uncertainty.

17.1 Structural uncertainty versus parameter uncertainty

Parameter uncertainty asks “what is the correct value of CD?” Structural uncertainty asks “is this drag law even the right form?” Both matter. Confidence intervals on fitted coefficients do not protect against a missing physics mechanism such as ventilation, flexible rocker or an unmodelled line-compliance mode.

17.2 Practical identifiability

Some parameters are strongly correlated. For example, increasing residual drag and decreasing line elevation can both raise horizontal tension in a straight run. To separate them, independently measure cable height and line geometry. Likewise, roll-dependent side force and rider lean can compensate each other in trajectory data, so board attitude must be measured directly.

17.3 Sensitivity priorities

Before spending effort on elaborate turbulence models, compute sensitivities of outputs to uncertain inputs. If peak take-off height is far more sensitive to release timing and line angle than to skin-friction coefficient, measurement effort should follow that hierarchy. This is one of the strongest arguments for a reduced model early in the project.

18. Proposed master-level research programme

Research question

How accurately can a reduced-order 6-DOF, cable-constrained planing model predict trajectory, tow-line tension and take-off impulse of a cable-park wakeboard rider across controlled edging manoeuvres?

Work packages

  1. WP1: geometry and kinematics. Survey a specific cable park and derive the carrier path, line geometry and corner curvature.
  2. WP2: instrumented experiments. Build a load-cell handle and synchronise IMU, GNSS and video.
  3. WP3: baseline hydro model. Implement steady planing support, friction, residual drag and empirical side-force maps.
  4. WP4: unsteady extension. Add added-mass and time-varying wetted-footprint terms.
  5. WP5: system identification. Fit parameters using straight runs and controlled edges only.
  6. WP6: blind validation. Predict aggressive progressive edges and simple take-offs not used in calibration.
  7. WP7: high-fidelity cross-check. Run a limited set of CFD/VOF cases to inspect pressure distribution and centre-of-pressure migration.

Potential thesis contributions

  • First cable-specific measured line-load and 6-DOF dataset for the chosen manoeuvres.
  • A validated reduced-order board-water force model for rolled/yawed cable wakeboarding.
  • A quantitative explanation of speed gain and line loading from moving-tether geometry.
  • A physically interpretable take-off impulse model for cable air tricks.
  • An open simulation architecture that can later support coaching, virtual prototyping or autonomous camera systems.

18.1 Candidate hypotheses

  • H1: rider speed during aggressive progressive edging is significantly larger than carrier speed and is predictable from moving-tether geometry plus a quasi-steady side-force model.
  • H2: the vertical component of cable tension reduces steady board loading enough that boat-derived horizontal-tow planing models systematically overestimate required hydrodynamic support.
  • H3: take-off vertical impulse cannot be predicted accurately from steady lift coefficients alone; an unsteady wetted-area / added-mass term is required.
  • H4: a calibrated coefficient-map model can predict line tension and trajectory across riders better than a single “edge force proportional to tan(phi)” law.

18.2 Minimum publishable dataset

A valuable open dataset would include synchronised raw line tension, board IMU, rider/board position, carrier position, board geometry, rider mass, cable speed, cable height, tow-line length and video for a set of repeatable manoeuvres. Publishing raw data and calibration metadata would enable independent models to be compared on the same benchmark.

18.3 What would constitute a strong thesis result?

Not a photorealistic animation. A stronger result would be a model that predicts independent experiments with quantified error, explains where and why it fails, and shows which added physical mechanism most reduces the error. For example, demonstrating that a 6-DOF quasi-steady model predicts trajectory well but under-predicts take-off impulse, and that an added-mass release term removes most of that discrepancy, would be a scientifically meaningful contribution.

19. Conclusions

Five conclusions matter most for simulation:

  1. The cable is a moving power source, not merely a prescribed speed. A taut line constrains radial relative motion, so the rider can swing and exceed carrier speed.
  2. The elevated tow point changes everything. Line tension directly unloads the board vertically and contributes to take-off impulse.
  3. Edging is a 3D planing problem. Roll and yaw create large lateral forces and moments, and the required hydrodynamic resultant rises rapidly with edge angle.
  4. Air-trick release is an impulse problem. The key variables are hydrodynamic reaction, centre of pressure, line tension, board attitude and contact-loss timing.
  5. Validation must drive model complexity. A calibrated reduced-order model with measured line load and motion is more scientifically useful than unvalidated CFD. CFD should be used to explain and improve the reduced model, not replace experimental identification.

Appendix B: implementation skeleton

# Pseudocode for a reduced 6-DOF cable-wakeboard simulator
state = initialise_state()
while t < t_end:
    carrier = cable_path.evaluate(t)
    line = tow_line.evaluate(carrier, state.handle_position, state.handle_velocity)

    water_state = contact_model.detect_water_contact(state.board_pose, state.board_velocity)
    hydro = hydro_model.evaluate(state, water_state)

    rider_control = controller_or_measured_motion(t, state)
    contacts = feature_contact_model.evaluate(state)

    forces, moments = assemble(gravity, line, hydro, rider_control, contacts)
    state = constrained_integrator.step(state, forces, moments, dt)

    detect_events(line_slack, takeoff, landing, feature_entry, feature_exit)
    log_energy_and_constraint_residuals()
